description_full: Global Industrial Company, through its subsidiaries, operates as an industrial distributor of various industrial and maintenance, repair, and operation (MRO) products in the United States and Canada. It offers storage and shelving products, safety and security products, carts and trucks, HVAC and fans, furniture and decor, material handling products, janitorial and facility maintenance products, workbenches and shop desks, tools and instruments, plumbing and pumps, office and school supplies, packaging and shipping products, lighting and electrical products, foodservice and retail products, medical and laboratory products, motors and power transmission products, building supplies, machining products, fasteners and hardware, vehicle maintenance products, and raw materials. The company distributes its industrial and MRO products under the Global, GlobalIndustrial.com, Nexel, Paramount, Interion, and Absocold brands. The company serves for-profit and not-for-profit businesses; state, local, and private educational organizations; and government entities, including federal, state, and local municipalities through relationship marketers, e-commerce sites, and catalogs. The company was formerly known as Systemax Inc and changed its name to Global Industrial Company in June 2021. Global Industrial Company was founded in 1949 and is headquartered in Port Washington, New York.
ceo_bio: Ms. Anesa T. Chaibi | CEO & Director | Age 59 | Compensation: $2.7M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $697K ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers, declining at 7%/yr — weakening productivity. Each employee generates $38K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Global Industrial Company is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.8B market cap on $1.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and -3% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 36% against a 10% cost of capital — a 26-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 34%.

The business throws off $75M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.08× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 52% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.64x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-8.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 65% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.06 vs 5y 0.93), so read it loosely.
About $5.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $43.43 (margin of safety -7%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 31%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $33.86 to $56.38 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 66% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $40.50 on average, 13% below the price.
The price implies 10.7% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 36% clears the cost of capital of 9.5% by 26pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.02).
It runs a 34% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.08x.
ROE of 23% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.6, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.0 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.8% over 3 years, 6.0% over 5 years and -2.9% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 41% of profits supports about 14.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 26%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 51.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 35%.
Insider trading is two-way: 4 purchases and 10 sales over the past year, net $1.2M sold.
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (0.4% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 10 consecutive years, though it has been cut 21.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,980 employees, each generates about $697K of revenue, 1.9x the Industrials median, and productivity has fallen 6.8% a year.
That works out to $38K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (4x revenue per employee).
